title: My First Game Using Generative AI: Seeking Depth and Physics Feedback
author: Happy-Fruit-8628
selftext:
Hey 
I am new to Ai game development and recently built a this game. The goal was to create a fast paced racing experience where player can drive different types of cars and drift builds across detailed tracks with smooth controls and responsive handling. The prototype currently includes sprint races, time trials and basic car selection along with some basic settings.

I built it using Tessala. What I am trying to improve now is not the visuals but the driving feel and overall gameplay depth. Generating tracks and cars works well, but making each car type feel distinct, especially when comparing drift focused cars to grip focused builds, has been more challenging. I have been iterating on prompts that describe physics behavior, traction differences, tuning values and progression systems, but I am still figuring out how much detail to include before it becomes too constrained. 

For those working with generative AI in game development, how do you approach prompting for mechanics heavy systems like racing physics? Do you define rule sets and constraints first and then layer the experience on top, or do you describe the complete player experience and refine it step by step? 

I have attached a short gameplay clip and would really appreciate honest feedback on the driving feel, pacing and how I could push the depth further.

comments.author: Abdullah_3254
comments.body:
Nice work for a first AI racing prototype. The speed feels good, but the cars seem a bit too similar in handling right now. You could probably push the difference between drift and grip builds more so each one has a clearer identity.

For physics prompting, I’d define the core rules first and then tweak the feel in small iterations instead of trying to describe everything at once. Overall solid base to build on.

comments.author: darkluna_94
comments.body: You might experiment a bit more with the physics to add some extra weight and depth to the movements but overall it’s genuinely impressive.

comments.author: Substantial_Dear
comments.body:
This is about how far I get with any 100% vibe-coded games. At some point you've got to get your hands dirty if you want a project to succeed.

I do wonder if AI will ever be able to produce that magic sauce that separates the good games from the bad.

replies.author: No-Difference629
replies.body: You should check my latest post on my page of my game footage then;) fully ai coded, I do not know how to code at all

replies.author: Odd_Law244
replies.body: To do that, it would need to be able to playtest them and understand what makes a game fun for humans to play. So we're probably a long ways off still.

comments.author: 88chilly
comments.body: Good start honestly the track gen looks solid. For racing physics I’ve found it helps to define the handling model first grip curve, weight transfer, accel vs traction limits and treat each car as just different values inside that same system. If you try to prompt the full feel at once it gets messy fast. Since Tessala.co already gives you the structure, I’d lock the base physics rules first then iterate per car with small parameter changes.

comments.author: ResenhaDoBar
comments.body:
I always build the games modularly with the full vision in mind.

If I’m making a racing game, step 0 is to get the car to move well, after we have a toy we can turn it into a game.

comments.body: feel like back to 20 years ago... GTA.....

comments.author: SlaughterWare
comments.body:
As a real dev, but not anti-ai, this is pretty impressive stuff! 
I wish someone would do a unity game and make it open source so I could observe how far they get. 
I don't think ai can do much beyond simple games yet. But we're not far off. 
Id definitely like to use it for building templates, just as a time saver if nothing else.
